plot_extraction.response_text:
Cantankerous Mr. Wragg’s attractive niece, Miss Miller, comes to live with him, drawing the attention of local young men—especially fisherman George Gale. Desperate to get close to her despite her uncle’s hostility, George follows his friends’ scheme to stage a bicycle accident outside the house. They carry him into Mr. Wragg’s bed and persuade a doctor that he is seriously injured.

The doctor orders George not to be moved and allows him only water. Realizing the accident was contrived, Mr. Wragg takes revenge by locking George in the bedroom, withholding his clothes and food, mocking his supposed delirium, and publicizing his predicament to the neighbors. Miss Miller eventually releases and feeds the humiliated George. When he declares that he must leave town to escape ridicule, she coyly suggests there may be a way for him to avoid looking foolish and maneuvers him into proposing marriage—only to teasingly pretend he is mad for suggesting it. When Mr. Wragg returns, he concludes that both of them are mad.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a brisk, lightly satirical comic style rooted in everyday life in a small English fishing community. Its humor arises from social embarrassment, courtship, practical jokes, and reversals of power rather than from broad fantasy or moral commentary. The setting is established economically through a few concrete details—the steep road, harbor, fishing boats, public house, and clustered neighbors—after which the narrative concentrates on interpersonal conflict. The result is a compact farce with a strong sense of village intimacy, where private foolishness rapidly becomes public entertainment.

The narration is third-person and broadly omniscient, moving freely among outward action, communal opinion, and the thoughts of individual characters, especially George Gale. The narrator maintains an amused emotional distance and rarely explains the joke directly. Instead, irony is embedded in apparently sober descriptions, as when Gale interprets eating only two herrings instead of four as evidence that he is “slowly fading,” or when his companions’ rough handling is presented as an attempt to restore his faculties. This mock-serious phrasing repeatedly elevates trivial or ridiculous events into matters of grave importance.

Characterization is economical and behavior-driven. Mr. Wragg is defined by irritability, possessiveness, quick malice, and verbal agility; Gale by physical confidence, romantic timidity, vanity, and gullibility; Harris and Brown by opportunistic mischief; and Miss Miller by apparent sweetness combined with a sharp enjoyment of teasing. The characters are comic types, but their motives remain recognizable. Status shifts continually: Gale begins by tormenting Wragg, becomes helpless once infatuated, and is then imprisoned and humiliated by the older man he had mocked. Miss Miller ultimately gains control of both men by alternately helping, scolding, encouraging, and misleading Gale.

Dialogue carries most of the story’s energy. It is rapid, adversarial, and built from taunts, evasions, repetitions, and literal-minded replies. Much of the comedy depends on one speaker maintaining a false premise while another becomes increasingly exasperated, most notably in Wragg’s elaborate insistence that fairies brought Gale to “Buckingham Pallis.” Exchanges often escalate through repeated words—“Coax? Coax?” or the extended “If—if—” sequence—so that rhythm itself becomes comic. Dialogue also functions as action: characters maneuver, deceive, flirt, and retaliate primarily through speech.

The spoken language is strongly differentiated from the polished narrative voice. Working-class and regional speech is represented through dropped initial consonants, eye dialect, contractions, and nonstandard grammar: “’ouse,” “’im,” “agin,” “dursen’t,” “arf,” and “a-purpose.” These features establish locality and class while giving the dialogue an audible, theatrical quality. The dialect is not rendered so densely that it obstructs comprehension; it supplies flavor, timing, and characterization. Wragg’s speech is especially effective because his rough pronunciation contrasts with the speed and inventiveness of his sarcasm.

Sentence structure in the narration is generally clear, balanced, and moderately formal. Longer sentences often arrange comic information in a sequence that delays the punch line, while short sentences sharpen reactions or reversals. Semicolons and coordinated clauses create a measured storytelling cadence, and precise adverbs such as “placidly,” “sententiously,” “respectfully,” and “gleefully” often expose a mismatch between a character’s manner and the absurdity of the situation. Understatement is central: violent, humiliating, or emotionally charged actions are described with controlled politeness, making them funnier.

The plot is tightly causal and progressively escalating. An initial clash between Wragg and Gale establishes their rivalry; Miss Miller’s arrival gives Gale a motive to seek entry into the house; the staged bicycle accident places him in Wragg’s bed; the doctor’s orders transform the prank into imprisonment; and the loss of Gale’s clothes completes his humiliation. Each development grows naturally from the previous one while worsening the predicament. Physical comedy—the trunk striking Wragg, the bicycle fall, the kick, the broken door handle—alternates with verbal comedy, preventing the narrative from becoming static.

A recurring technique is dramatic irony. The reader understands Gale’s deception, then watches it escape his control; later Gale gradually realizes that Wragg and Miss Miller understand more than they pretend. Objects such as the trunk, bicycle, bed, clothes, water jug, and locked door become mechanisms of reversal. Food is another comic motif: Gale’s supposedly lovesick appetite, the doctor’s water-only prescription, the tantalizing discussion of chicken and port, and the eventual cold beef all convert romantic longing into bodily discomfort.

The pacing is fast but carefully staged. Brief descriptive transitions compress days or summarize village reactions, while major comic scenes unfold through detailed dialogue and incremental escalation. Pauses, overheard voices, closed doors, and delayed entrances create near-theatrical timing. The reader is repeatedly allowed to anticipate disaster just before it occurs, and scenes commonly end on a fresh humiliation or change in advantage.

The tone remains genial despite the cruelty of the practical joke. Injuries and threats are stylized rather than disturbing, and the narrative assumes a resilient social world in which mockery is part of communal life. Sentiment is continually punctured by appetite, vanity, or ridicule. Even the apparent romantic resolution is overturned: Miss Miller’s blushes encourage Gale to propose, only for her to declare him mad. The final sentence extends the joke by reporting Wragg’s judgment that both young people are insane, closing the story on symmetrical exasperation rather than conventional romance.

Overall, the style is best characterized as concise social farce: formally controlled narration, vivid colloquial dialogue, understated irony, sharply drawn comic types, and a mechanically precise sequence of misunderstandings and reversals. Its dominant effect comes from treating foolish behavior with grave narrative composure while allowing the characters’ voices to supply noise, conflict, and comic momentum.

## A Guest at Wragg’s

Mr. Wragg’s cottage stood halfway up the steep road from Bellwick Harbour, where it could obtain smoke from the chimneys above, tar from the boats below, and every piece of news before it had travelled fifty yards in either direction. It was a narrow house, with a brass knocker too large for the door and two front windows which Mr. Wragg cleaned every Saturday and looked through during the remainder of the week.

He was looking through one of them when George Gale came up from the harbour carrying one end of a sea-chest. Ned Harris carried the other, and Sam Brown walked behind offering advice.

“Lift your end, George,” said Harris.

“I am lifting it.”

“Then lift mine.”

Mr. Wragg opened the window.

“Take that thing off my pavement,” he said.

George stopped. He was a broad young fisherman with cheerful blue eyes and the settled belief that age had been created to furnish youth with amusement.

“What thing?” he asked.

“That great ugly box.”

Harris lowered his end thoughtfully. George, taken by surprise, retained his; and the chest swung round and struck Mr. Wragg’s wall with a report which brought two women to neighboring windows.

“Mind my ’ouse!” shouted Mr. Wragg.

“Your house moved,” said George. “I saw it.”

“It moved when you hit it.”

“Then it ought to be more careful.”

Mr. Wragg, who had spent sixty years sharpening a natural gift for unpleasant reply, looked from George to the chest.

“Whose is it?” he demanded.

“Sam’s uncle’s.”

“Then put Sam’s uncle inside and throw ’em both in the harbour.”

Brown laughed so heartily that he walked backward into the chest. George and Harris, inspired by his example, lifted it suddenly, and one corner caught Mr. Wragg, who had emerged to defend his property, with sufficient firmness to seat him on his own doorstep.

The young men apologized at once. Harris took off his cap, Brown brushed Mr. Wragg’s sleeve, and George inquired whether he had hurt the step.

“You wait,” said Mr. Wragg, rising. “You wait, George Gale. I’ll get even with you one o’ these days.”

George looked respectfully up and down the road.

“Where shall I wait?” he asked.

Mr. Wragg went indoors and closed the door with such vigor that the brass knocker struck twice. The young men continued uphill, and by evening the story had reached the King’s Arms in three forms, all of them unfavorable to Mr. Wragg’s dignity.

For a week he saw no opportunity of repaying George. At the end of that time a cab stopped outside his cottage, and the driver lowered a brown trunk which, by a regrettable coincidence, struck the same doorstep.

A young woman descended after it.

She was Mr. Wragg’s niece, Miss Lucy Miller, who had come from London to keep house for him. Before she had been in Bellwick two hours the harbor knew her name, the color of her eyes, the probable value of her hat, and the fact that she had refused three offers of assistance between the station and the cottage. Before she had been there two days, the young men of Bellwick had developed an interest in Mr. Wragg which he found both sudden and suspicious.

George Gale developed the strongest interest of all.

He first saw Miss Miller on the following morning, when she stood in the doorway shaking a tablecloth. The wind carried one corner over her head and displayed a small, laughing face beneath it. George, who had weathered gales in the North Sea without losing either his balance or his appetite, walked into a fish basket.

Miss Miller withdrew indoors. Mr. Wragg appeared in her place.

“You done that basket any good?” he asked.

“I was looking at the weather,” said George.

“Ah. Weather generally comes from the sky, but perhaps it’s altered.”

George kicked the basket aside and went down to his boat. At dinner he ate only two herrings instead of four, a circumstance which caused his mother to feel his forehead and his father to remark that no good came of sitting up late at public houses.

During the next few days he passed Mr. Wragg’s cottage so often that even the road seemed surprised. Sometimes Miss Miller was at the window; sometimes Mr. Wragg was. The difference became plain before George reached the gate. Miss Miller smiled. Mr. Wragg picked up things.

One evening George paused to admire a geranium in the front garden.

“Pretty flower,” he said, as Mr. Wragg came out.

“Which one?”

“That red one.”

“It’s a brick.”

“I meant the one behind it.”

“That’s a broken pot.”

George considered the garden more carefully.

“You don’t want any help with it, do you?” he asked.

“Yes,” said Mr. Wragg. “I want somebody to stand outside and keep fools away.”

George leaned on the gate.

“Your niece settling down all right?”

“She was till now.”

“London must be very different from Bellwick.”

“It is. There’s more room there for you to keep away from ’er.”

George straightened himself.

“I’m only being neighborly.”

“Then go and be neighborly to somebody else.”

He slammed the gate. The latch caught George’s fingers, and Miss Miller, appearing at the window, laughed. George walked down the road with a face of great composure until he reached the corner.

That night at the King’s Arms he placed the matter before Harris and Brown. He did not say that he wanted to court Miss Miller. He said merely that a friendly call was one of the ordinary duties of civilized life, and that Mr. Wragg, by preventing it, was placing himself outside society.

“Knock at the door,” said Brown.

“He’d shut it.”

“Put your foot in.”

“He’d break it.”

Harris, who had been listening with his head on one side, looked toward the yard, where his bicycle leaned against the wall.

“Suppose you was took ill outside his ’ouse?” he said.

“Wragg would send for the undertaker.”

“Suppose you was hurt?”

“He’d finish it.”

“Not with Miss Miller there,” said Harris. “Women won’t let injured people lie in the road. It’s against their nature.”

George looked doubtful.

“What sort of injury?”

“Bicycle accident,” said Harris. “I lend you mine. You ride down the hill, fall off at Wragg’s gate, and me and Sam carry you in.”

“I can’t ride.”

“So much the better. It’ll look natural.”

Brown put down his mug. “There’s a doctor coming to see old Mrs. Pike at seven to-morrow. We fetch him. He says George mustn’t be moved. George stays in the ’ouse, Miss Miller nurses him, and old Wragg boils.”

George’s eyes brightened.

“How long do I stay?”

“That,” said Harris, “depends on how badly you fall.”

They arranged the details with great care. George was to coast down the hill shortly before seven, apply the brake opposite Mr. Wragg’s gate, and lie still. Harris and Brown were to be close behind. They spent half an hour deciding which leg should be injured, and another quarter deciding that the head offered greater freedom.

“You can’t forget and walk on your head,” Brown explained.

The following evening was clear and calm. At six fifty-five Mr. Wragg sat in his parlor reading the newspaper, while Miss Miller sewed by the window. The road outside was unusually well attended. Harris examined a wall fifty yards uphill; Brown waited below, studying the harbor; and five boys lingered opposite with the air of persons expecting history.

At six fifty-eight George appeared at the top of the road on Harris’s bicycle.

He had intended to coast slowly. The road intended otherwise. He came down with his knees wide apart, his elbows trembling, and his eyes fixed upon Mr. Wragg’s gate. Harris shouted to him to use the brake. George replied that he was using everything he could find.

The bicycle gathered speed. Mr. Wragg, attracted by the shouting, reached the gate just as George reached it from the opposite direction. George turned the handle sharply. The bicycle struck the curb, rose with unexpected intelligence, and deposited him among the geraniums.

There was a short silence.

“Beautiful,” said Brown, hurrying up. “Couldn’t have done it better.”

George, whose shoulder had encountered the broken pot, opened one eye.

“Get me inside,” he whispered.

Harris knelt beside him.

“Don’t speak, old man,” he said loudly. “Save your strength.”

Mr. Wragg pushed through the gate. “Save his strength for what?”

“He’s badly hurt,” said Brown.

“He’s ruined my garden.”

Miss Miller came running out. She gave one glance at George’s pale and solemn face, and another at the twisted bicycle.

“Oh, uncle, we must take him in.”

“No,” said Mr. Wragg.

“He may be dying.”

“Then he can die where he fell. He chose the place.”

George closed both eyes and gave a faint groan which surprised even himself.

Miss Miller bent over him. “Can you hear me, Mr. Gale?”

He opened his eyes just far enough to see her.

“Mother,” he murmured.

“His mother’s six foot tall and weighs fourteen stone,” said Mr. Wragg. “He knows better.”

“Uncle!”

Harris and Brown lifted George. Their method of carrying an injured man was to seize whichever part came nearest. George’s head struck the gatepost, and his left boot caught Mr. Wragg in the stomach.

“He’s delirious,” said Harris, when Mr. Wragg complained.

“I’ll make ’im worse.”

They bore George into the cottage. Mr. Wragg attempted to direct them toward the kitchen settle, but Miss Miller, observing that it was narrow, led the way upstairs to the best bedroom. In another minute George was placed in Mr. Wragg’s own bed, his boots resting affectionately upon the white counterpane.

“My bed!” gasped Mr. Wragg.

“It’s the nearest,” said Miss Miller.

“It’s the furthest. The settle’s downstairs.”

“Don’t excite him,” said Brown.

“Excite ’im?”

“He may have internal injuries.”

“I’ll give ’im some external ones.”

The arrival of Dr. Price interrupted this promise. Harris fetched him from Mrs. Pike’s, and the doctor entered with the brisk resignation of a man accustomed to finding accidents wherever he was least wanted.

He examined George’s head, felt his pulse, moved his arms, and asked him several questions. George answered feebly, selecting at random from ailments he had heard discussed by elderly relatives.

“Pain here?” asked the doctor, pressing his ribs.

“Terrible.”

The doctor pressed on the other side.

“Here?”

“Worse.”

“Any dizziness?”

“Everything goes round.”

Mr. Wragg, standing at the foot of the bed, looked at the ceiling as though hoping it might fall.

The doctor straightened.

“No bones broken,” he said. “Severe shock, possibly concussion. He must remain perfectly quiet.”

“Where?” asked Mr. Wragg.

“Here.”

“Here?”

“He must not be moved to-night. Keep the room quiet and cool. Nothing to eat.”

George’s expression changed slightly.

“Nothing?” said Miss Miller.

“Water only. If he becomes restless or talks wildly, don’t be alarmed. It may be delirium.”

Mr. Wragg’s face became thoughtful.

“When can ’e be moved?” he asked.

“I’ll call in the morning.”

The doctor left. Harris and Brown followed after shaking George’s hand with funereal tenderness.

“Good-bye, old chap,” said Brown.

“Bear up,” said Harris.

George watched them go with a growing suspicion that they were enjoying themselves. Miss Miller arranged the pillows beneath his head. Her fingers were cool, her voice gentle, and George decided that the evening had been well spent.

Mr. Wragg stood beside the bed.

“You comfortable?” he asked.

“Not very,” said George, remembering his condition.

“I’ll see what I can do.”

He drew the blanket up to George’s chin, tucked it firmly beneath the mattress, and went out. Miss Miller followed to fetch water.

Mr. Wragg returned alone carrying the bicycle lamp.

“So you fell off,” he said.

George closed his eyes.

“Can’t talk.”

“Doctor said you would.”

“Head’s bad.”

“Use another one.”

George breathed heavily.

Mr. Wragg sat on a chair and regarded him with patient malice.

“Funny thing,” he said. “Harris’s bicycle having a lamp when Harris told Bill Thompson at six o’clock that ’e’d lent it to you.”

George’s breathing became less regular.

“Funny thing, too, Brown telling everybody at the King’s Arms there’d be an accident outside my place at seven.”

George opened his eyes.

“Did he?”

“He did. Delirious, ain’t you?”

“Very.”

“Good. I like a cheerful invalid.”

Miss Miller came in with a jug and glass. Mr. Wragg immediately assumed concern.

“Poor young feller,” he said. “Don’t know where ’e is.”

George looked at Miss Miller.

“Where am I?” he asked weakly.

Mr. Wragg answered before she could.

“Buckingham Pallis.”

Miss Miller bit her lip.

“Am I—am I the King?” George inquired.

“No,” said Mr. Wragg. “You’re the Queen’s aunt. Drink your water.”

George drank. Miss Miller told him to sleep and left the room. Mr. Wragg remained until his niece’s steps had died away; then he rose, took George’s clothes from the chair, and rolled them into a bundle.

“What are you doing?” demanded George.

“Taking care of your things. Delirious people eats their clothes sometimes.”

“Put ’em back.”

Mr. Wragg smiled.

“You’re in my bed, young George, and doctor says you can’t move. If you get up, you confess there’s nothing wrong with you. If you stay, you stay as I choose. Pleasant dreams.”

He went out with the clothes and locked the door.

George sat up. His head was sore from the genuine portion of the accident, his shoulder ached, and the room contained nothing edible. He examined the bedside table and found a Bible, a button, and Mr. Wragg’s false teeth in a tumbler.

At nine o’clock Miss Miller brought more water.

“Could I have a little bread?” George asked.

“The doctor said nothing but water.”

“Doctors say things in a general way.”

“Uncle says we must obey him exactly.”

“Your uncle,” said George, “is enjoying this.”

Miss Miller’s eyes widened.

“Enjoying your dangerous illness?”

“He knows.”

“Knows what?”

George looked at her closely. Her face was innocent, though one corner of her mouth appeared to require discipline.

“That the accident wasn’t altogether an accident.”

She set down the jug.

“Oh! Then you came off a-purpose?”

“The wheel turned.”

“Wheels often do.”

“I meant to fall,” admitted George, “but not quite so thoroughly.”

“And all to get into uncle’s house?”

George became modest.

“I wanted to see somebody.”

“Uncle?”

“No.”

“Me?”

George looked at the blanket.

Miss Miller blushed very prettily. “I think it was a foolish, deceitful trick.”

“So do I now.”

“And you deserve to be punished.”

“I’m being punished.”

“You have a comfortable bed.”

“I’ve had six glasses of water.”

“Water is good for you.”

“Not in those quantities. I can hear the tide turning inside me.”

She laughed, took the candle, and wished him good night. George called after her, but the key turned in the lock.

At half past nine Mr. Wragg’s voice sounded below.

“He’s asleep now, Mrs. Green. Poor chap. Doctor says ’e’s wandering in ’is mind.”

Mrs. Green’s voice answered from the passage.

“Fancy! And such a fine young man.”

“Ah, there’s often very little inside the biggest parcels.”

A second neighbor arrived, then a third. Mr. Wragg gave each a report in the doorway, raising his voice so that no symptom should be lost upstairs.

“Thinks ’e’s at Buckingham Pallis,” he said. “Calls me the Dook of Wellington. Tried to eat the soap. Doctor says it’s a most peculiar case.”

George climbed out of bed and crossed the room. The door was locked. He tried the window and found that it opened above the front gate, where seven neighbors were collected.

A small boy saw him.

“There ’e is!” he shouted.

Every face turned upward. George retired so quickly that he struck his shin against a chair.

“Get back to bed!” called Mr. Wragg. “You ain’t got no wings.”

Laughter rose from the road. George returned to bed and pulled the blanket over his head.

In the morning Dr. Price called early. Mr. Wragg admitted him with grave satisfaction and accompanied him upstairs.

The doctor found George’s pulse excellent and his temper less so.

“How do you feel?”

“Hungry.”

“A good sign. Any dizziness?”

“Only when people talk to me.”

The doctor smiled. “You may get up this afternoon if you feel steady. Light food first. An egg, perhaps, or a little broth.”

“He shall have water,” said Mr. Wragg. “It agreed with ’im beautiful.”

“Something light,” repeated the doctor. “And no excitement.”

When he had gone, George held out his hand.

“My clothes.”

“What clothes?” asked Mr. Wragg.

“The clothes I came in.”

“You came in by fairy magic. Fairies don’t wear clothes.”

“I’ll get out of this bed.”

“Do. There’s twelve people opposite waiting to see you.”

George crossed to the window. The cluster outside included Harris, Brown, Mrs. Green, two fishermen, five children, and the landlord of the King’s Arms. Harris waved.

“How’s Buckingham Pallis?” he called.

George closed the window.

At breakfast Mr. Wragg sent up another jug of water. At dinner, he carried a chair into the passage and discussed his meal with Miss Miller immediately outside the locked door.

“That chicken smells good,” he said loudly.

“It’s only cold beef,” said Miss Miller.

“Same thing to a man with imagination. Pass the pickles.”

There was a pause.

“Port wine would go well with this,” he continued.

“We haven’t any port.”

“We might pretend. George is doing well on pretending.”

A knock sounded from inside the bedroom.

“What is it?” called Miss Miller.

“Food.”

“Coax ’im,” said Mr. Wragg.

“What?”

“Coax ’im to eat his water.”

“I don’t want water!” shouted George.

“There,” said Mr. Wragg. “Delirious again. Says ’e don’t want water. Fish refusing water is serious.”

“I’m not a fish!”

“Doesn’t know his own trade.”

By mid-afternoon George’s romance had assumed the character of a military siege. He had eaten nothing since the previous day, unless one counted half a peppermint found in the pocket of Mr. Wragg’s dressing gown. He had considered escaping in the gown, but the crowd outside had increased after news spread that he believed himself to be a member of the Royal Family.

Harris and Brown called at three. Mr. Wragg admitted them.

“Can we see him?” asked Harris.

“If you don’t mind being recognized as angels.”

They entered the room with solemn faces. Brown placed two fingers on George’s wrist, and Harris stared closely into his eyes.

“Poor fellow,” said Brown.

“Get my clothes,” said George.

“Listen to him,” said Harris. “Always loved clothes.”

“You pair of swine planned this.”

“Memory’s coming back.”

“You go downstairs and make Wragg give me my things.”

Brown shook his head. “We dursen’t interfere with the doctor.”

“The doctor says I can get up.”

“Not without clothes,” said Harris reasonably.

George reached for him. Harris avoided the hand and moved to the foot of the bed.

“We’ll tell everybody you’re improving.”

“I’ll tell everybody you helped.”

“Delirium,” said Brown.

“Two black devils,” said George.

Harris opened the door. “He’s worse, Mr. Wragg!”

George flung the water glass. Harris ducked; it struck Brown on the ear. His companions, observing that excitement might retard his recovery, held him down and thumped his pillow until he became comparatively quiet. They then left, promising to call again.

That evening the door handle came off in George’s hand. He had twisted it in the hope of forcing the lock; the square iron bar slid free, leaving him with a brass knob and no immediate use for it. He threw it on the bed and addressed Mr. Wragg through the hole.

“You’ll have to let me out now.”

“Why?”

“Handle’s broken.”

“Then you can’t get out.”

“What if there’s a fire?”

“I’ll bring you some water. You’ve plenty of practice.”

Miss Miller came up after dark. She waited until her uncle went down the road to the King’s Arms, then unlocked the door.

George stood before her wrapped in the bed quilt, Mr. Wragg’s dressing gown being insufficient in several important directions.

“I brought you some beef,” she said.

He seized the plate and ate with a concentration which allowed no room for courtship. Miss Miller watched him cut slices of cold beef with the edge of a spoon.

“You might chew it,” she suggested.

“I can chew later.”

She had also brought bread, cheese, and a cup of tea. George disposed of them and sat back with a sigh.

“I was slowly fading,” he said.

“You seemed very strong when you threw the glass at Mr. Brown.”

“That was the last flare of life.”

She regarded him with amusement.

“You’d better go before uncle comes back.”

“In this?”

“Your clothes are in the kitchen cupboard. I’ll fetch them.”

She returned with the bundle and turned her back while he dressed. Mr. Wragg had knotted every garment separately and then tied the knots together. George worked at them in silence.

“There are people outside,” Miss Miller said.

“How many?”

“Only nine.”

“I can’t go through the front.”

“You could use the back.”

“The back way comes out beside the King’s Arms yard.”

“That is convenient. Your friends are there.”

George paused with one trouser leg in his hand.

“I shall leave Bellwick,” he said bitterly.

“Because of a little joke?”

“Little? By to-morrow every soul in the place will call me Queen Victoria.”

“They might forget.”

“They won’t. Fishermen remember a joke longer than they remember a debt.”

Miss Miller sat on the window ledge.

“It does look rather foolish,” she admitted.

George stared at her.

“Thank you.”

“Coming into a man’s house by pretending to be hurt merely because you wanted to see a young woman.”

“I know what I did.”

“And being put to bed and fed on water.”

“I know that too.”

“And losing your clothes.”

“Have you anything fresh?”

“No. I was only wondering whether there might be some way of making it look less foolish.”

George stopped working at the knots.

“What way?”

Miss Miller looked down. “If—if people thought you had some good reason for wanting to see the young woman.”

“They know I wanted to see you.”

“Yes, but if—if it was understood that you were serious.”

“I am serious.”

“If—if you weren’t just making yourself ridiculous for amusement.”

“I wasn’t amused.”

“If—if there were some proper explanation afterward.”

George gazed at her bent head. A blush had risen to her cheeks. His own face changed slowly from despair to astonished hope.

“You mean,” he said, “if you and me—”

“If what?”

“If we were—”

“If we were what?”

“You know.”

“I don’t.”

George swallowed. He had faced winter seas with more confidence than he now faced Miss Miller’s eyelashes.

“If I asked you to marry me,” he said.

She looked up quickly.

“Mr. Gale!”

“You said—”

“I said nothing of the kind.”

“You said if—if—”

“If what?”

“If people thought I had a reason.”

“So you ask every girl you make a fool of yourself over to marry you?”

“No. I never made a fool of myself over anybody else.”

“That is not very flattering.”

“I mean—Lucy, you know what I mean. I’ve been trying to speak to you ever since you came. I’ve walked past this house till my boots are half worn out. I’ve been thrown off a bicycle, starved, locked up, and called the Queen’s aunt. If that doesn’t show I’m serious, nothing will.”

Miss Miller’s expression softened.

“Do you truly want to marry me?”

“Yes.”

“Even after uncle’s treatment?”

“I’m not marrying him.”

“He may come to live with us.”

George hesitated for one fatal instant.

Miss Miller drew herself up. “I see.”

“No, no. Let him come. We’ll have a room ready.”

“With a lock outside?”

“With two, if he likes. Lucy, will you?”

She looked toward the door. Steps sounded below, followed by the scrape of Mr. Wragg’s key in the front lock.

“Quick,” whispered George. “Say yes.”

“After knowing you one week?”

“It’s been a long week.”

“After such deceitful behavior?”

“I’ll never have another bicycle accident.”

“And while you’re in uncle’s bedroom, dressed in clothes stolen from his cupboard?”

“They’re my clothes!”

“You are getting excited,” she said anxiously. “The doctor warned us.”

George stared at her.

“What?”

“You must lie down.”

“Lie down?”

“Perhaps you’re delirious again. You imagined I wanted you to propose.”

“You made me!”

“Made you?”

“You went on saying ‘if—if—’ till there was nothing else a man could do.”

Miss Miller moved toward the door.

“I’m afraid you are very ill.”

George caught her hand.

“You little rogue,” he said. “You knew.”

“Knew what?”

“That I’d ask.”

“Let go. Uncle’s coming.”

“Not till you answer.”

“I have answered. I think you’re mad.”

Mr. Wragg’s footsteps sounded on the stairs.

George lowered his voice. “Will you marry me?”

“No.”

“Will you?”

“No.”

“Lucy!”

Miss Miller tried to free her hand, laughing in spite of herself. George drew her closer; she pushed him away; and at that moment Mr. Wragg entered carrying a paper parcel and an expression of suspicion.

He stopped.

George stood in the middle of the room with one trouser leg properly arranged and the other tucked into his boot. The quilt lay on the floor. Miss Miller was flushed and laughing, and both her hands were held in George’s.

Mr. Wragg looked at the empty plate, the open door, and the clothes.

“What’s all this?” he demanded.

“He’s delirious,” said Miss Miller, snatching her hands away.

“Delirious?”

“He thinks I’m going to marry him.”

Mr. Wragg turned slowly to George.

“Marry ’er?”

“She put it into my head,” said George.

“I did not!”

“You said there was a way to stop people laughing.”

“I said there might be.”

“And then you said ‘if’ about twenty times.”

“I was trying to be kind.”

“Kind!” exclaimed George. “Coaxing a starving man into proposing and then calling him mad!”

“Coax?” said Miss Miller. “Coax?”

“Yes, coax.”

“I never coaxed you.”

“You coaxed every word out of me.”

Mr. Wragg looked from one to the other.

“Stop,” he said. “I want to understand. You”—he pointed at George—“pretended to break your neck to get into my ’ouse.”

“Yes.”

“You let yourself be put in my bed.”

“Yes.”

“You lived on water, lost your clothes, and had half Bellwick laughing at you.”

“Yes.”

“And now you want to marry the girl that helped do it?”

George looked at Miss Miller. She was trying to appear offended, but the corners of her mouth betrayed her.

“Yes,” he said.

Mr. Wragg turned to his niece.

“And you unlocked the door, fed ’im, gave ’im back ’is clothes, and then talked to ’im till ’e proposed?”

“I did not talk him into anything.”

“You said ‘if,’” George reminded her.

Miss Miller stamped her foot.

Mr. Wragg backed toward the door. His usual readiness of speech had deserted him. He regarded George’s disordered clothes, his niece’s blushes, the broken handle, the empty beef plate, and the bicycle lamp still standing on the chest of drawers.

Then he shook his head.

“Doctor was wrong,” he said. “It ain’t only him. You’re both mad.”

He went out and locked the door behind him.

For a moment the young people stared at it.

Then George turned.

“Well?” he said.

Miss Miller sat on the edge of the bed.

“Well what?”

“There’s no handle, and he’s got the key. We may be here some time.”

“That is your fault.”

“Most things seem to be.”

She smiled.

Outside, Mr. Wragg’s voice was already audible at the front gate, informing Mrs. Green that the patient had developed a second and even more alarming delusion. Inside, George sat beside Miss Miller and resumed the discussion from the point at which it had been interrupted.

By the time Mr. Wragg returned with Harris and Brown as witnesses, George had received an answer. Miss Miller, however, denied this so sweetly, and George contradicted her so warmly, that Mr. Wragg’s original medical opinion remained unaltered.

The Clockmaker of Bellweather

Every clock in Bellweather stopped at 3:17 on the morning Elias Vale died.

The town did not notice immediately. At that hour, the bakers were still asleep, the fishermen had not yet reached the harbor, and even the old women who swept their doorsteps before dawn were dreaming behind shuttered windows.

Only Mara Vale was awake.

She sat beside her father’s bed in the room above the clock shop, listening to the rain tap against the glass. Elias had been ill for months, though he never named the illness. He called it “a little rust in the gears” and smiled whenever Mara asked whether they should send for the doctor.

That night, his breath grew thin and irregular. The lamp flame trembled with each draft.

“Open the window,” he whispered.

“It’s raining.”

“I know.”

Mara lifted the latch. Cold air spilled into the room, carrying the scent of wet stone, chimney smoke, and the sea. Far below, Bellweather’s streets shone under the lamps.

Elias turned his face toward the open window.

“Can you hear them?” he asked.

Mara heard rain, gutter water, and the distant groan of boats against their ropes.

“Hear what?”

“The clocks.”

There were more than two hundred clocks in the shop below them. Tall clocks, carriage clocks, brass clocks, painted clocks, clocks that sang at noon and clocks whose faces showed the phases of the moon. Mara had grown up amid their ticking. To her, the sound was not noise but weather, constant and enveloping.

Now she listened carefully.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

“They’re running,” she said.

“For the moment.”

Elias’s hand moved across the blanket, searching. Mara took it. His fingers were cool and strangely light.

“You must not repair the silver clock,” he said.

She glanced toward the cabinet in the corner. Inside stood a clock she had never seen running: a narrow silver instrument with no numbers on its face, only a ring of tiny engraved stars. It had belonged, Elias once told her, to the first clockmaker in Bellweather.

“Why not?”

“Because some things are broken for a reason.”

He closed his eyes.

Mara waited for him to say more. Instead, every clock below struck once.

The sound rose through the floorboards like thunder.

Then came silence.

Elias Vale died at 3:17 in the morning, and time in Bellweather stopped with him.

At first, the silence seemed to belong only to the shop.

Mara descended the stairs holding a candle. The clocks crowded the dark room, their hands all pointing to 3:17. She wound a walnut mantel clock. Its key resisted. She opened the case of a tall black clock and nudged the pendulum. It swung once, twice, then stopped.

She tried another, and another.

None would run.

At dawn, Tomas Reed, the baker, arrived carrying a loaf wrapped in linen. He removed his hat when he saw Mara’s face.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “Your father was a good man.”

Then he noticed the clocks.

“Mine has stopped too,” he added. “So has the one above the oven. Thought it was the heat.”

By seven, a crowd had gathered outside.

Every clock in Bellweather showed 3:17.

The clock in the church tower had stopped. The harbor clock had stopped. Pocket watches, kitchen clocks, and cheap tin alarm clocks had stopped. Even the sundial in the market square seemed useless, for the rain continued and the sun did not appear.

Yet morning came. The sky brightened. People grew hungry. Children woke and asked why the school bell had not rung.

The mayor ordered the church bell sounded eight times. School began, shops opened, fishing boats departed, and Bellweather attempted to continue.

But a town without clocks soon discovers how much faith it has placed in them.

Bread burned. Meetings started too early or too late. Fishermen missed the turning tide. The noon train arrived to find no passengers waiting, then departed with the stationmaster running beside it, waving his cap. Arguments spread through the market.

“It’s nearly four.”

“It cannot be four. I only just ate.”

“You always eat late.”

“How late?”

No one knew.

After Elias’s funeral, the mayor visited the shop with the priest, the stationmaster, and three members of the town council. They stood beneath the motionless clocks while rain streaked the windows.

“You are the clockmaker now,” the mayor said.

Mara was nineteen, and although she had repaired clocks since childhood, no one had ever called her that.

“I suppose I am.”

“Then repair them.”

“I’ve tried.”

“Try harder.”

The priest frowned at him.

The mayor cleared his throat. “Naturally, grief has made the work difficult. But the town depends upon you.”

Mara looked at the faces surrounding her. They were not cruel faces. They were frightened.

“Bring me your clocks,” she said. “I’ll do what I can.”

For three days and three nights, she worked.

She cleaned springs, replaced gears, polished pivots, and balanced pendulums. She repaired faults that should have stopped clocks years earlier. Still, whenever she set a clock in motion, its hands returned to 3:17 and froze.

On the fourth night, exhausted, Mara fell asleep at her father’s workbench.

She dreamed of him standing on the harbor wall.

Behind him, the sea had withdrawn beyond the horizon, revealing a vast plain of black mud. Thousands of clocks lay half-buried in it, ticking beneath a red sky.

“You must not repair the silver clock,” he said again.

“Then tell me how to repair the others.”

Elias looked toward the empty sea.

“I already did.”

She woke to the sound of ticking.

Mara sat upright.

The shop was dark except for moonlight. For the first time since her father’s death, the clouds had parted. Pale light streamed through the front window and fell upon the silver clock in the cabinet.

Tick.

Its hands had appeared.

Mara approached slowly. During the day, the silver clock’s face held only engraved stars. Now two delicate hands shone beneath the glass. They pointed to 3:17.

Tick.

The longer hand moved backward.

3:16.

Mara remembered her father’s warning. She also remembered the mayor’s frightened face and the fishermen standing helplessly at the harbor.

She unlocked the cabinet.

The silver clock was cold when she lifted it. There was no keyhole, no hinge, and no seam in its casing. On the back, words had been engraved in a script so fine she had to carry it to the window.

WHAT IS TAKEN MAY BE RETURNED.

WHAT IS RETURNED MUST BE TAKEN.

Below the inscription was a shallow hollow shaped like a human thumb.

Mara pressed it.

The clock sprang open.

Inside, instead of gears, she saw darkness scattered with points of light. It seemed deeper than the casing, deep enough to contain a winter sky. At its center turned one tiny golden wheel.

A folded note lay beside it.

Mara recognized her father’s handwriting.

My dear Mara,

If you are reading this, then I have failed to convince you with a warning alone. That is my fault. Warnings without explanations are merely invitations.

The clock belonged to Amiel Bell, founder of our town. He made it after losing his wife in a storm. He believed time was a substance, like water, and that moments could be stored, removed, or poured back into the world.

He was correct.

But time is never given freely. To extend one hour, the clock must shorten another. To restore a day, it must take a day from somewhere—or someone.

For many years, the clock remained dormant. Then, when you were six, you fell from the eastern cliff.

Mara stopped reading.

She remembered the cliff only in fragments: white gulls, crumbling earth, her father shouting her name. She remembered waking in bed with both arms broken. Everyone said she had landed on a narrow ledge.

The letter continued.

You did not land on the ledge. You fell into the sea. By the time I reached you, you were gone.

I used the clock to take back nine minutes.

The price was not clear at first. Soon afterward, clocks began losing seconds. Winter arrived early. Flowers withered before blooming. People forgot conversations they had only just begun. I realized the clock had taken the nine minutes from Bellweather itself, dividing the debt among every living thing.

I stopped it, but the debt remained. Year by year, I paid what I could from my own life. It was not enough.

When I died, the clock claimed the remaining balance all at once.

Bellweather has not lost time, Mara. It has been caught inside the nine minutes I stole.

Do not repair the silver clock. If you free the town, it will demand payment from you.

Forgive me.

Mara read the letter three times.

Outside, the moon hung above the rooftops. No clouds moved across it. The rainwater dripping from the eaves seemed to fall too slowly, each drop stretching like glass.

Bellweather had not merely lost the ability to measure time. The town itself was slowing.

The next morning—or what everyone agreed to call morning—Mara walked to the harbor.

The tide had not changed.

Boats that should have returned the previous evening remained at sea. A gull hovered above the pier, beating its wings without advancing. Along the shore, waves held their shapes for several breaths before collapsing.

“How long can this continue?” asked Tomas Reed, who had closed his bakery after his yeast stopped rising.

Mara thought of the silver clock.

“I don’t know.”

“Can you fix it?”

She looked across the harbor at the stalled horizon.

“Yes,” she said. “But I don’t know what it will cost.”

News spread quickly.

By afternoon, the council chamber was full. Mara placed the silver clock on the long table and read her father’s letter aloud. No one interrupted.

When she finished, the mayor removed his spectacles.

“This is absurd.”

At that moment, the clock ticked backward.

Every candle flame bent toward it.

No one called the story absurd again.

“If it wants time,” said the stationmaster, “we can give it time.”

“How?” asked Tomas.

“From all of us. There are three thousand people in Bellweather. Nine minutes divided among us is nothing.”

“It has already taken nine minutes from everyone,” Mara said. “My father believed the debt had grown. Interest, perhaps. Or the clock charges more when time is moved twice.”

“How much more?”

“I don’t know.”

The room filled with murmurs.

The priest raised a hand. “Can the payment be divided?”

“My father’s letter says it will demand payment from me.”

“Because you’re the clockmaker?”

“Because I opened it. Or because I’m the one who was saved.”

The mayor stood. “Then close it.”

“And leave the town trapped?”

“Better trapped than dead.”

“We don’t know that anyone will die.”

“We know nothing,” he snapped. “That is precisely the problem.”

An old woman named Agnes Wren rose from the back row. She had delivered half the children in Bellweather and buried two husbands.

“How many years might it take?” she asked Mara.

“I can’t say.”

“I have four or five I could spare.”

Her daughter protested, but Agnes ignored her.

“I would give one.”

“So would I,” said Tomas.

Others spoke. Some offered a year, some a month, some a single day. Several said nothing. The mayor stared at the table.

Mara carried the silver clock home with a list of 127 names.

That night, she studied the clock under lamplight.

The golden wheel inside it turned backward. Around its edge were tiny symbols. She recognized them from her father’s oldest notebooks: marks for breath, blood, memory, sleep, and age.

One symbol was shaped like an open hand.

Beneath it, almost invisible, was a narrow lever.

Mara touched the lever with a pair of tweezers.

A voice spoke from the clock.

“Name the hour.”

The voice belonged to no man or woman. It sounded like rain falling upward.

Mara nearly dropped the tweezers.

“What hour?”

“Name the hour to be returned.”

“The hour after 3:17.”

“Name the payment.”

She unfolded the list.

“Agnes Wren offers one year.”

The clock’s stars brightened.

“Insufficient.”

“Tomas Reed offers one year.”

“Insufficient.”

She read every name. The offered years amounted to thirty-four years, seven months, and twelve days.

“Insufficient.”

“How much do you want?”

The clock ticked.

“All that followed.”

Mara’s mouth went dry. “What does that mean?”

“All that followed the stolen hour.”

“My life?”

“All that followed.”

She thought of her childhood after the fall. Thirteen years of school mornings, summer swims, burnt pies, skinned knees, arguments, songs, and quiet evenings beside her father. Thirteen years that should never have existed.

“If you take those years,” she whispered, “will I die?”

“Death is not the only absence.”

The clock closed.

Mara sat alone until the lamp went out.

Over the following days, Bellweather slowed further.

Voices deepened and stretched. Soup would not boil. A falling cup took long enough to reach the floor that its owner caught it after crossing the room. People slept and woke uncertain whether minutes or nights had passed.

Beyond the town limits, time continued normally.

The noon train flashed through the station like a silver arrow, no longer stopping. Rain clouds raced overhead, but Bellweather felt only a few drops. Ships appeared on the horizon and vanished before harbor workers could raise a signal.

Some residents tried to leave.

They returned minutes later, though they claimed to have been gone for days. At the northern road, soldiers from the capital erected a barrier. To the outside world, Bellweather had become a place of blurred figures and drawn-out bells, dangerous to approach.

Mara spent long hours in her father’s room, reading his notebooks.

Near the end of the final volume, she found an entry written shortly before his death.

A clock does not measure time. It measures change. The swing of a pendulum, the decay of a spring, the movement of a shadow—these are changes we agree to call seconds.

If Amiel’s machine asks for “all that followed,” perhaps it does not mean years.

Perhaps it means change.

Below the paragraph, Elias had drawn the open-hand symbol.

Mara understood.

The clock did not want her life. It wanted the person she had become during the stolen years: her memories, her skills, her love, her grief. If she paid, she might live—but the Mara who remembered Elias would be gone.

She carried the silver clock to the church tower.

The climb took hours, or perhaps only minutes. It was impossible to tell. At the top, she found the great iron mechanism motionless beneath the bell.

From there she could see all of Bellweather.

People stood in the square, barely moving. The harbor water was smooth as polished stone. In the east, dawn and sunset seemed to exist together, gold light on one horizon and violet darkness on the other.

Mara placed the silver clock inside the church clock’s mechanism.

It opened at once.

“Name the hour,” said the voice.

“The hour after 3:17.”

“Name the payment.”

Mara closed her eyes.

She remembered her father teaching her to hold a screwdriver. Never force it, he had said. Listen to what the metal wants.

She remembered him carrying her home after she broke her arms, his coat soaked with seawater.

She remembered winter evenings when they drank bitter chocolate in the shop. Her first repaired watch. His applause. Their arguments. His illness. His last breath.

“All that followed,” she said.

“Accepted.”

“Wait.”

The golden wheel paused.

“If you take my memories, take this one last: Elias Vale saved me because he loved me. The debt is mine, but the choice was his. Let Bellweather remember him kindly.”

“The hour does not bargain.”

“I’m not bargaining.”

“Then release the hand.”

Mara had not noticed that she was holding the lever.

She let go.

The silver clock struck.

Its sound was small, no louder than a spoon touching glass.

Then the church bell answered.

Across Bellweather, every clock leaped forward.

Pendulums swung. Springs tightened. Wheels turned. The harbor tide crashed against the seawall. Wind rushed through streets in a single enormous breath. Candles flared, dogs barked, and every person in the square stumbled as the world regained its proper speed.

The silver clock dissolved into a cloud of bright dust.

Mara fell.

When she opened her eyes, strangers surrounded her.

A broad man in a flour-covered coat held her hand. An old woman touched her forehead. The priest was praying. The mayor stood nearby, weeping without dignity.

“Who are you?” Mara asked.

The broad man made a broken sound.

“It’s Tomas,” he said. “You know me.”

She did not.

They told her her name. They told her where she lived. They told her she was a clockmaker.

“I don’t know anything about clocks,” she said.

No one knew how to answer.

In the years that followed, Bellweather became famous.

Scientists came to examine the clocks, though they found nothing unusual. Officials collected testimonies. Newspapers printed wild accounts of a town that had fallen outside time.

The people of Bellweather rarely spoke to visitors about Mara Vale.

She continued living above the clock shop. Tomas and Agnes taught her how to cook, how to read, and how to find her way through town. Children brought her flowers. Customers came not for repairs but to sit with her and explain, again and again, who she had been.

She listened politely.

On the wall above the workbench hung a portrait of a gray-haired man with gentle eyes.

“Who is he?” she often asked.

“Your father,” someone would say. “Elias Vale.”

Mara would study the portrait and nod, though the name awakened nothing in her.

Years passed.

Then, one spring morning, a little girl entered the shop carrying a broken music box.

“My mother says no one can fix it,” the girl said.

“She’s probably right,” Mara replied.

“Could you try?”

Mara took the box. Its painted lid showed a ship beneath a silver moon. She turned it over in her hands.

Without thinking, she chose a screwdriver from the workbench.

She opened the case and examined the mechanism. One tooth on the smallest gear was bent. Her fingers moved with confidence she did not understand.

“Never force it,” she murmured. “Listen to what the metal wants.”

The girl leaned closer. “Who taught you that?”

Mara froze.

For an instant, she smelled rain and seawater. She heard hundreds of clocks ticking in darkness. A hand, cool and light, closed around hers.

Then the sensation vanished.

“I don’t know,” she said.

She straightened the tooth, wound the spring, and closed the case.

Music filled the shop.

At that same moment, every clock in Bellweather struck 3:17, though it was nearly noon. The sound rolled over the rooftops and out across the harbor.

People stopped where they were.

Mara looked up, startled, as bells and chimes and cuckoos called from every corner of the town. Yet no one appeared afraid.

Outside the shop, Tomas Reed removed his hat. Agnes Wren smiled. The mayor, older now and walking with a cane, bowed his head.

The clocks finished striking.

For one breath, Bellweather was silent.

Then every clock resumed its ticking, and this time none of them stopped.
